title: Read-Write Lock
summary:
A read-write lock has two modes over the same data.

- **Write lock: blocks everyone.** Take it when you change the content.
- **Read lock: shared.** Any number of readers hold it at once, but it **blocks writers until every reader is done**. Take it when you must not see data changing under you: while you hold a read lock, the content cannot change.

**Waiting policy matters.** A reader-preferring lock lets new readers in while others read, so a steady stream of readers can **starve a writer**. A **writer-preferring** lock (the convention used here) blocks *new* readers as soon as a writer is waiting; the writer runs when the readers already inside finish. It protects writers at the price of delaying new readers.

```
R1, R2 hold read lock → W arrives, waits → R3 arrives, queued behind W
R1, R2 release → W runs alone → W releases → R3 runs
```

- **Worth it when** reads vastly outnumber writes and the read section is long enough that parallel readers pay off.
- **Not worth it** for write-heavy data or tiny critical sections: the bookkeeping makes a plain mutex faster.
- **Never upgrade** from read to write while holding the read lock: the writer waits for all readers, including you. Release, then take the write lock and re-check.

The same contention rules apply as for any lock ([lock contention](#/sd/f/lock-contention)); the protocol is in [acquire / release](#/sd/f/acquire-release).

drills.q: Under a writer-preferring read-write lock, put these events in the order each caller gets to run: R1 and R2 are reading when W arrives, then R3 arrives.
items: R1 and R2 read in parallel
W requests the write lock and waits for R1 and R2
R3 requests the read lock and is queued behind W
R1 and R2 release; W runs alone
drills.explain: Writer preference blocks R3 even though other readers are currently inside. If readers were preferred, R3 would join immediately and a steady stream of readers could delay W forever.

drills.q: A cache refresh job (writer) needs the lock, but readers arrive constantly and the writer never runs. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: A reader-preferring lock is starving the writer; use writer preference or a fair lock
The lock should be replaced by a distributed lease
drills.explain: With reader preference, new readers keep getting in as long as any reader is in, so the count never reaches zero. Making new readers wait once a writer queues bounds the writer's wait.

drills.q: A thread holds a read lock and calls `writeLock.acquire()` on the same lock, intending to upgrade. What happens?
options: It deadlocks: the writer waits for all readers to leave, and the thread is one of them
It succeeds because it is the same thread
The read lock is released automatically first
drills.explain: The write lock needs zero readers, and this thread is a reader waiting on itself. Release the read lock, take the write lock, then re-validate what you read, because it may have changed in between.

drills.q: Four readers hold a read lock from t = 0 ms, each for 10 ms, in parallel. A writer requests the lock at t = 1 ms. The lock is writer-preferring and no other reader arrives. How long does the writer wait before it gets the lock, in milliseconds?
drills.explain: The writer must wait until the last active reader finishes at t = 10 ms; it arrived at t = 1 ms, so it waits 9 ms. Readers that arrive after t = 1 ms would be blocked behind the writer.

drills.q: A service updates a shared lookup table on 50% of its requests, and each critical section is a few microseconds. Would you use a read-write lock?
options: Probably not: with frequent writes and tiny sections, a plain mutex is simpler and often faster
Yes: read-write locks are always faster than mutexes
No: read-write locks can't protect tables
drills.explain: The benefit comes from many readers overlapping with few writers. Here readers rarely overlap, while the extra bookkeeping and writer handoffs cost more than they save.

drills.q: Explain read and write lock semantics, including which side the lock favors and why.
drills.answer: Many readers can hold the read lock together, but the write lock is exclusive: it needs no readers and no other writer. While a read lock is held, the data cannot change. A writer-preferring policy makes new readers wait once a writer is queued, so writers are not starved by a continuous stream of readers; the cost is that new readers can be delayed.
